title: Hospital and primary care outcomes following universal nirsevimab immunization in infants in Puglia, Italy: a population-based observational study
abstract: Abstract Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections and hospitalization in infants. In 2024, the Puglia Region introduced universal infant immunization with nirsevimab, providing an opportunity to assess its real-world impact on RSV-related outcomes across both hospital and primary care settings. Aims To evaluate the effectiveness of nirsevimab in reducing RSV-related hospitalizations and disease severity during the 2024–2025 RSV season compared with the 2023–2024 season, and describe the burden and clinical characteristics of bronchiolitis reported in primary care. Results Following the introduction of nirsevimab, RSV-related hospitalizations declined from 931 to 259 cases (3.71% vs. RSV-related hospitalization rates were 71% lower in 2024–2025 than in 2023–2024; equivalently, infants in the 2023–2024 seasonal population had a 3.45-fold higher hospitalization risk (RR 3.45, 95% CI 3.01–3.96; p p Conclusions In this regional real-world setting, universal nirsevimab implementation was associated with substantially lower RSV-related hospitalization rates. The primary care survey also indicated a lower reported burden of clinically diagnosed bronchiolitis, although patient-level effectiveness could not be estimated from aggregate survey data.

title: The role of Andrographis herb (Andrographidis herba) in the treatment of viral respiratory tract infections
abstract: Wstęp Choroby zakaźne pozostają znacznym obciążeniem dla systemów opieki zdrowotnej, co jest potęgowane przez narastający problem oporności na leki przeciwdrobnoustrojowe. Sytuacja ta wymusza poszukiwanie bezpiecznych alternatyw terapeutycznych o szerokim spektrum działania, w tym z wykorzystaniem fitoterapii. Jedną z roślin, która w ostatnim czasie wzbudziła szczególne zainteresowanie badaczy z całego świata, jest brodziuszka wiechowata (Andrographis paniculata (Burm. Pozyskiwany z niej surowiec – ziele brodziuszki (Andrographidis herba) – wykazuje wiele właściwości przeciwwirusowych i immunomodulujących. Cel pracy Celem niniejszej pracy był przegląd literatury naukowej oraz podsumowanie obecnego stanu wiedzy na temat zastosowania preparatów z ziela brodziuszki w leczeniu wirusowych infekcji dróg oddechowych, ze szczególnym uwzględnieniem syncytialnego wirusa oddechowego (RSV), wirusów grypy, koronawirusów (w tym SARS-CoV-2) oraz nieswoistych infekcji wirusowych. Metodyka wyszukiwania i doboru piśmiennictwa Przegląd piśmiennictwa oparto na przeszukaniu baz danych: Google Scholar, PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus oraz Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Wyszukiwanie literatury przeprowadzono przy użyciu następujących haseł: „Andrographis paniculata”, „andrographolide”, „COVID-19”, „RSV”, „Respiratory Syncytial Virus”, „influenza”, „upper respiratory tract infection”, „common cold”, „antiviral”, „clinical trial”, „double blind”, „quadruple blind”, „in vitro”, „in vivo”, „drug resistance”, „phytochemistry”. Wyniki Przeanalizowana literatura wskazuje, że ekstrakty z ziela brodziuszki, a w szczególności ich główny związek aktywny – andrografolid, wykazują właściwości przeciwzapalne oraz aktywność przeciwwirusową wobec wirusów wywołujących infekcje dróg oddechowych, w tym wirusów grypy i SARS-CoV-2. Dane kliniczne potwierdzają ich skuteczność w łagodzeniu nasilenia i skracaniu czasu trwania objawów w nieswoistych infekcjach górnych dróg oddechowych. W kontekście łagodnych przypadków COVID-19 dotychczasowe obserwacje są obiecujące, jednak ostateczne dowody kliniczne pozostają wciąż niewystarczające, natomiast doniesienia o aktywności wobec wirusów grypy i RSV opierają się obecnie na danych przedklinicznych, przy czym wyniki dotyczące hamowania namnażania RSV są niejednoznaczne. Ogólny potencjał terapeutyczny jest wyraźnie ograniczony, głównie ze względu na słabą rozpuszczalność w wodzie i niską biodostępność ogólnoustrojową aktywnych fitozwiązków, co wskazuje na konieczność opracowania nowych systemów dostarczania leków. Wnioski Preparaty z ziela brodziuszki mogłyby stanowić wartościową terapię wspomagającą w łagodnych, nieswoistych infekcjach dróg oddechowych, jednak ostateczne potwierdzenie ich skuteczności klinicznej wciąż wymaga przeprowadzenia szeroko zakrojonych, wieloośrodkowych prób. Rozwiązaniem omijającym problem niskiej biodostępności systemowej związków czynnych ziela brodziuszki może być opracowanie preparatów o działaniu miejscowym (np. Taka postać leku pozwala na osiągnięcie odpowiedniego stężenia terapeutycznego w obrębie błon śluzowych dróg oddechowych, dodatkowo ograniczając ryzyko wystąpienia ogólnoustrojowych działań niepożądanych.

Jedną z roślin, która w ostatnim czasie wzbudziła szczególne zainteresowanie badaczy z całego świata, jest brodziuszka wiechowata (Andrographis paniculata (Burm. title: A-363 Comparison of comprehensive syndromic versus limited respiratory panel results in a point-of-care setting
abstract: Abstract Background Syndromic multiplex molecular point-of-care (POC) tests boast high sensitivity and short turnaround times, supporting prompt diagnosis and informed treatment decisions at the time of patient visit (Lucar 2024). The family of BIOFIRE® SPOTFIRE® Respiratory/Sore Throat (R/ST) Panels are such tests with options for a comprehensive syndromic panel (R/ST Panel) and a condensed menu panel (R/ST Mini) limited to five viral pathogens: Influenza A and B viruses, human rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The comprehensive R/ST Panel has four additional viral pathogens, the ability to subtype influenza A/H1-2009 and A/H3, and four atypical bacterial pathogens (see Figure 1). When utilizing these types of POC tests appropriately, positive results can reduce antibiotic use, increase appropriate antiviral prescriptions, and may reduce hospitalization time (Schneider 2020, Egilmezer 2018). These outcomes ultimately improve diagnostic stewardship by eliminating the need for serial or individual testing. This analysis demonstrates how the respiratory menu for R/ST Panel Mini and the comprehensive R/ST Panel can increase diagnostic yield. Methods Deidentified patient test results were captured by BIOFIRE® FIREWORKSTM Trends (Trends), a cloud-based pathogen surveillance network for BIOFIRE® systems. Results were limited to 01/01/2025 to 01/31/2026 for the comprehensive R/ST Panel with the nasopharyngeal sample type. The diagnostic yield for all pathogens on the R/ST Panel was compared to the theoretical diagnostic yield for a subset of pathogens present on the R/ST Panel Mini over the course of 2025. Peak pathogen activity was also summarized and compared over time. Results During respiratory season, detection of R/ST Panel Mini pathogens were highest with an average diagnostic yield of 51.8%, and lowest during the late spring and summer months (diagnostic yield = 43.3%). In contrast, the R/ST Panel with all pathogens results in a diagnostic yield of 65.5% during the respiratory season and 56.8% during spring and summer months. The three most common pathogens identified on the comprehensive R/ST Panel that are not included on the R/ST Panel Mini include parainfluenza virus, seasonal coronaviruses, and adenovirus, with >2,500 detections from each virus. Many of these detections occur in the late spring and early summer, after the peak influenza season. Conclusion When respiratory virus transmission is high and contextual and/or operational constraints exist, the SPOTFIRE® R/ST Panel Mini detects five common respiratory viruses, which supports rapid clinical decision-making for patient treatment and management. In the months outside of respiratory season, the comprehensive syndromic SPOTFIRE® R/ST Panel improves diagnostic yield by 14% on average (range: 5% - 22%). The comprehensive SPOTFIRE® R/ST Panel therefore offers robust syndromic testing in a point-of-care setting, which may reduce the need for additional follow ups, improving diagnostic stewardship and patient management.

title: Disseminated BCG disease and recurrent pulmonary infections in a child with trisomy 21 carrying a novel BACH2 variant of uncertain significance: a 5-year case report
abstract: Background Trisomy 21 is associated with combined immune dysregulation, including lymphopenia, impaired responses to vaccines, and heightened susceptibility to respiratory infections, driven in part by triplication of chromosome 21-encoded interferon receptor genes. BACH2 haploinsufficiency is a rare monogenic immunodeficiency characterized by lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and susceptibility to infections and autoimmune diseases. Co-occurrence of these two conditions has not been previously described. Case presentation We report a 5-year longitudinal course in a Kenyan girl with trisomy 21, congenital heart disease, aspiration, and severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) found via whole exome sequencing to carry a heterozygous BACH2 missense variant (c.1420C > G;p.Leu474Val) of uncertain significance; parental segregation remains incomplete. In silico protein structural modeling (FoldX and Missense3D) yielded discordant predictions of the variant's effect on the protein’s stability and structure. Additional in silico pathogenicity predictions were also inconsistent: Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (SIFT), Evolutionary Model of Variant Effect (EVE), PolyPhen-2, and CADD Phred scores predicted pathogenicity, while REVEL and AlphaMissense suggested a lack of deleteriousness. Persistent panlymphopenia and profoundly low IgM levels were documented throughout the follow-up period. Over these 5 years, the girl sustained six hospitalized lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), with four requiring intensive care, which were disseminated Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) disease, respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2 infections, and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 pneumonia. Chest computed tomography at 4 years showed bilateral consolidations without bronchiectasis. Annual autoimmune screening remained negative. Conclusion This case illustrates the burden caused by severe and diverse respiratory pathogenic infections in a child with trisomy 21 and a candidate BACH2 variant. Trisomy 21 alone plausibly explains much of the phenotype; an independent contribution from the BACH2 variant remains unproven pending functional and segregation studies. Clinical considerations supported by this case include the potential value of prevaccination immunological screening to prevent BCG disease, equitable access to viral prophylaxis, and early specialist engagement in refractory cases.

source_records.abstract: Background Trisomy 21 is associated with combined immune dysregulation, including lymphopenia, impaired responses to vaccines, and heightened susceptibility to respiratory infections, driven in part by triplication of chromosome 21-encoded interferon receptor genes. BACH2 haploinsufficiency is a rare monogenic immunodeficiency characterized by lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and susceptibility to infections and autoimmune diseases. Co-occurrence of these two conditions has not been previously described. Case presentation We report a 5-year longitudinal course in a Kenyan girl with trisomy 21, congenital heart disease, aspiration, and severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) found via whole exome sequencing to carry a heterozygous BACH2 missense variant (c.1420C > G;p.Leu474Val) of uncertain significance; parental segregation remains incomplete. In silico protein structural modeling (FoldX and Missense3D) yielded discordant predictions of the variant's effect on the protein’s stability and structure. Additional in silico pathogenicity predictions were also inconsistent: Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (SIFT), Evolutionary Model of Variant Effect (EVE), PolyPhen-2, and CADD Phred scores predicted pathogenicity, while REVEL and AlphaMissense suggested a lack of deleteriousness. Persistent panlymphopenia and profoundly low IgM levels were documented throughout the follow-up period. Over these 5 years, the girl sustained six hospitalized lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), with four requiring intensive care, which were disseminated Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) disease, respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2 infections, and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 pneumonia. Chest computed tomography at 4 years showed bilateral consolidations without bronchiectasis. Annual autoimmune screening remained negative. Conclusion This case illustrates the burden caused by severe and diverse respiratory pathogenic infections in a child with trisomy 21 and a candidate BACH2 variant. Trisomy 21 alone plausibly explains much of the phenotype; an independent contribution from the BACH2 variant remains unproven pending functional and segregation studies. Clinical considerations supported by this case include the potential value of prevaccination immunological screening to prevent BCG disease, equitable access to viral prophylaxis, and early specialist engagement in refractory cases.

title: Multiplex real-time pcr for detection of respiratory viruses in pediatric cystic fibrosis patients: viral-bacterial co-infection patterns and clinical associations in Tehran, Iran (2023–2024)
abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) patients are at increased risk for respiratory complications from viral infections. This study evaluated the prevalence of Influenza A/B, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 in pediatric CF patients and characterized viral-bacterial co-infection patterns during the post-COVID-19 period in Tehran, Iran (2023–2024). A total of 113 respiratory samples were collected from pediatric CF patients (aged 2.5 months to 18 years). Viral RNA was extracted and analyzed using a multiplex TaqMan-based real-time PCR assay targeting SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A/B, and RSV. Bacterial/fungal co-infections were identified by standard microbiological culture. Viral pathogens were detected in 19 samples (16.81%); Influenza A/B was the only virus detected among the pathogens included in the multiplex PCR panel. All viral-positive cases occurred in patients experiencing pulmonary exacerbation (32.8%; p -value < 0.0001), with no significant associations with gender ( p -value = 0.322), age group ( p -value = 0.26), or season ( p -value = 0.50). Bacterial/fungal co-infection was detected in 89.47% of viral-positive cases, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the most common pathogen (47.4%). No bacterial or fungal genera showed significant association with influenza infection. Influenza A/B detection was significantly associated with pulmonary exacerbation episodes in this cohort. Although no significant association was observed between bacterial/fungal colonization with the phase of the disease, the importance of this matter cannot be overlooked. Routine multiplex PCR testing during exacerbation may improve disease management in this population.

title: Elucidation of the roles of IRF9 and IFI6 in RSV Cytopathogenesis
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of severe lung disease in young infants, the elderly, and immunocompromised people. It causes symptoms ranging from runny noses to life threatening bronchiolitis and pneumonia. The World Health Organisiation estimates that RSV infects >60 million infants worldwide and causes >160,000 deaths annually. Despitate its clinical impotance, there are no RSV vaccines or specific therapeutics. To develop effective drugs against RSV disease, it is essential to understand how RSV interacts with its target cells, the human airway epithelium. The Power Lab have established novel authentic models of RSV infection of paediatric airway epithelium based on primary airway epithelial cell cultures that look and behave like airway epithelium in infants.In a potentially major breakthrough, by comparing gene transcription profiles from RSV-infected airway epithelium cultures derived from cohorts of healthy infants with histories of severe or mild RSV disease, the Power Lab identified a number of genes that may be associated with disease severity. This PhD thesis investigated two of these genes, IRF9 and IFI6, in detail to determine their role in RSV cytopathogenesis and whether they have potential as biomarkers of severe RSV disease.

title: QMini: A Portable Device for Infectious Disease Testing
abstract: Abstract Widespread testing identifies infectious diseases early and reduces silent transmission. The large size of devices for testing limits their use in the field. We developed a portable device that miniaturizes nucleic acid testing: the QMini. The QMini simplified a fluidic module using direct connections between pumps and reaction chambers. It shielded an optical module from ambient light with a 3D-printed enclosure. We applied the QMini to detect synthetic nucleic acid sequences of respiratory syncytial virus B, SARS-CoV-2, and influenza A with a bead-based assay using quantum dot barcodes. The QMini detected 500 copies of respiratory syncytial virus B, 500 copies of SARS-CoV-2, and 1,000 copies of influenza A. We observed limited cross-reactivity in the QMini with six nontarget viral nucleic acid sequences. The QMini advances the portability of nucleic acid testing using quantum dot barcodes through device miniaturization.

title: Inflammasomes and interferons: new insights into the innate immune response to RSV and SARS-CoV-2 infection in airway epithelial cells
abstract: Respiratory viruses like RSV and SARS-CoV-2 pose significant public health threats, particularly to the young and elderly. Both viruses infect the airway epithelium, with severe disease associated with enhanced highly inflammatory immune responses. To develop novel therapeutics there is an urgent need to understand how specific innate immune responses are activated and regulated by RSV and SARS-CoV-2. Inflammasomes are cytosolic protein complexes that mediate the maturation and release of the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 and pyroptotic cell death. Given inflammasomes trigger potent inflammation that correlates with disease severity, we hypothesised that inflammasome activation may be critical. Inflammasome research has focused primarily on myeloid cells and NLRP3, herein we investigated inflammasome signalling within the airway epithelium using physiologically relevant well-differentiated primary airway epithelial cell cultures (WD-PAECs). We found that although the canonical inflammasome NLRP1 is constitutively expressed and infection upregulates inflammasome-related genes, direct infection-induced activation is minimal. However, crosstalk between epithelial and immune cells significantly potentiates this response. Despite dysregulated inflammasome activation being associated with disease severity, inflammasome activation, in addition to the interferon response was shown to play an important role in cell intrinsic antiviral responses. We demonstrated that IL-1β, bolstered by epithelial-myeloid interactions, plays a crucial role in early antiviral defence against RSV, making inflammasome activation a double-edged sword. Given co-infections account for >30% of all respiratory viral infections, we explored the interactions between RSV and SARS-CoV-2. Our findings revealed bi-directional viral interference patterns, driven by time-dependent induction of type I interferons (IFNs), highlighting their underappreciated role in the airway epithelium's innate armoury. By utilizing primary cell models, this work provides new insights into how the airway epithelium regulates innate immunity and highlights the complex balance between protective antiviral signalling and harmful inflammation during viral infection and co-infection. Thesis is embargoed until 31 July 2027.

title: Is Wastewater Surveillance Predictive during the Endemic Phase of Respiratory Disease? An Analysis Based on Clinical, Wastewater, and Digital Search Data in Detroit, Michigan
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has emerged as a major public health innovation catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic. However, its potential remains underexplored during and after COVID-19’s transition to endemicity. This study evaluates WBE’s potential to identify the COVID-19 pandemic-to-endemic transition and to provide early warnings across multiple surveillance systems for influenza A (IAV) and B (IBV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 in the postpandemic era. We monitored SARS-CoV-2 N1 concentrations in wastewater from April 8, 2020, and July 31, 2025, generating the earliest and longest-running wastewater dataset in Detroit, MI. A peak identification method was implemented to identify the pandemic-to-endemic transition by comparing the frequency of N1 concentration peaks between phases. During the endemic phase, from October 1, 2022, and March 31, 2025, we monitored RSV, IAV, IBV, and SARS-CoV-2 in Detroit’s wastewater. Pearson correlations were implemented to quantify the associations between wastewater concentrations and clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological data. Time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) was used to examine temporal dynamics among these datasets and identify the earliest emerging data for each disease and time lags. Extensive literature studies were conducted to elucidate the time-lag mechanisms for each disease, embracing the TLCC results. Random forest models were established to predict clinical cases based on WBE datasets. This was among the first studies using WBE-based approaches to identify pandemic-to-endemic transition of SARS-CoV-2. The relationships of wastewater data to traditional clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological surveillance data were systematically analyzed during the endemic phase of these respiratory diseases. This study demonstrates the predictive value of WBE during the endemic phase, providing early warnings and predictions for seasonal respiratory diseases, including COVID-19, influenza, and flu-like disease.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation of Influenza A virus mRNAs
abstract: The fate of cellular mRNAs is governed by intricate and dynamic post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms that fine-tune cellular gene expression. Processes such as stabilisation, degradation, splicing, nuclear export and RNA editing, are essential for mRNA processing and are known to be hijacked by RNA viruses to enhance their own gene expression. It is well established that influenza A virus (IAV) exploits these pathways as a means to increase viral gene expression, replication and pathogenesis. However, many questions remain surrounding the precise mechanisms behind these interactions. The work presented in this thesis reveals novel insights into mechanisms driving IAV mRNA post-transcriptional regulation. Chapter 1 begins with a review of post-transcriptional regulatory processes utilised by four enveloped respiratory viruses: Influenza A virus (IAV), Human Parainfluenza virus (hPIV), Respiratory Syncytial virus (RSV) and Severe Respiratory Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2). Chapter 2 presents an investigation into the epitranscriptomic landscape of IAV mRNAs, with a focus on N-6-methyladenosine (m6A) and pseudouridine (Ψ), two of the more abundant RNA modifications for cellular mRNA. Internal base modifications are dynamic regulators of RNA and play crucial roles during the lifecycle of both cellular and viral RNA. title: Paediatric airway epithelium in health and disease: "comparative responses of airway epithelium from healthy and wheezing children to viral and allergen insult”.
abstract: Asthma affects 300 million children worldwide. Early age viral infection and allergen sensitization are associated with subsequent asthma development. We aimed to understand the consequences of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and/or house-dust mite (HDM) exposure on cytopathogenesis, virus replication, and innate immune responses in airway epithelium from young children. Well-differentiated primary nasal epithelial cell (WD-PNEC) cultures were derived from newborn infants and pre-school children (aged 1-6) and identified as; 1. mild wheezers, and 3. severe wheezers [n=5 each]). They were infected with RSV following HDM stimulation. Virus growth kinetics, WD-PNEC cytopathology, innate immune responses, and effects of HDM treatment on IGF1R and nucleolin expression were analysed. RSV infected WD-PNECs derived from either newborn and/or pre-school children resulted in similar growth kinetics regardless of age and wheeze phenotype. Interestingly, HDM pre-treatment significantly delayed viral growth between 24-48 hpi, independent of wheeze phenotype, but virus titres at 96 hpi were similar. While RSV infection resulted in significant cell loss across all age groups, cilia loss in WD-PNECs from severe wheezers in the pre-school cohort was most profound. HDM pre-treatment did not alter innate immune responses to infection. Expression of IL-29 and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), including Ifi6, Isg15, Duoxa2, Duox2, were significantly increased following infection, as were CEACAM1, TRAIL, CX3CL1, GM-CSF, CXCL8, and CXCL16 protein secretions. Interestingly, IRF9, IFI6, and ISG15 expression were significantly lower in mild compared to severe wheezers or healthy individuals. Furthermore, CEACAM1 and IL-33 secretions were highest, and GM-CSF was lowest, in WD-PNECs from severe wheezers. Surprisingly, genes associated with asthma and airway remodelling, including TSLP, HMGB1, and KRT5, were reduced following RSV infection in all cohorts. Moreover, Western blot and IF analysis of total IGF1R, PKCζ, and Nucleolin (important for RSV attachment/entry) showed a partial reduction following HDM treatment compared to DMEM controls at 3 hpi. These data may explain, in part, the attenuated RSV growth kinetics evident in WD-PNEC cultures pre-treated with HDM. However, although differential gene/protein expression was observed in children with no, mild or severe wheeze, the functional consequences of these responses on the progression of wheeze pathogenesis remain to be determined.

title: Case Report: When muscle edema is not a myositis flare: Legionella pneumonia complicated by rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury in long-standing polymyositis
abstract: Legionella pneumophila is an important cause of severe community-acquired pneumonia and can produce extrapulmonary manifestations that obscure the primary diagnosis. Diagnostic error is especially likely in patients with established idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, because fever, myalgia, weakness, creatine kinase elevation and muscle edema may be attributed to autoimmune flare. We report a 70-year-old woman with a 25-year history of polymyositis receiving long-term corticosteroids and azathioprine who developed high fever, severe bilateral thigh pain and progressive proximal weakness after recent travel. On transfer, she had anuria with bladder distension, dark urine, diffuse posterior-thigh muscle edema, pneumonia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, myoglobinemia and acute kidney injury. Legionella pneumonia with rhabdomyolysis and multifactorial acute kidney injury was suspected clinically, and Legionella-active antimicrobial therapy, hydration, urinary drainage and urine alkalinization were started before microbiological confirmation. title: From Evidence to Implementation: The Added Value of Health Economics for RSV Immunisation Implementation in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in young children. In 2019, RSV was estimated to cause approximately 33 million acute lower respiratory infections, 3.6 million hospitalisations and more than 101,000 deaths among children under five years of age, with more than 97% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The recent availability of a maternal RSV vaccine and long-acting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) provides new opportunities to prevent severe disease during early infancy. This thesis investigates how epidemiological and health economic evidence can support the implementation of RSV immunisation strategies, with particular emphasis on LMICs. Epidemiological studies first examined RSV burden, seasonality and the age distribution of severe disease. In the Netherlands, RSV circulation was substantially disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, including an unusual summer epidemic in 2021, but subsequently returned towards its pre-pandemic winter pattern. Severe disease remained concentrated in young infants. Importantly, 6% of RSV-related hospitalisations among infants aged <1 year occurred within the first 14 days of life, highlighting the importance of timely protection after birth. The RSV GOLD III–ICU Network Study subsequently investigated severe respiratory infections among children aged <2 years across ten LMICs. During local RSV seasons, 29.0% of children admitted with severe respiratory illness tested positive for RSV. Most life-threatening RSV infections occurred among infants aged <6 months, with almost half occurring during the first three months of life, demonstrating the potential for early-life immunisation to prevent severe disease. Cost-of-illness studies in Mozambique and Nepal demonstrated that RSV also imposes a substantial economic burden. In Mozambique, mean costs increased from USD 612 for severe hospitalised disease to USD 1,161 for life-threatening disease requiring intensive care. Household costs represented approximately 43–145% of the monthly minimum wage. In Nepal, mean total costs were USD 312 for hospitalised cases and USD 664 for intensive-care cases, with substantial out-of-pocket expenditure relative to the monthly minimum wage. Cost-effectiveness analyses evaluated maternal vaccination and long-acting mAbs over 2025–2034. In Nepal, maternal vaccination at USD 5 per dose was estimated to prevent approximately 2,500 deaths and 50,000 hospitalisations, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of USD 387 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. A mAb at the same price could prevent approximately 2,400 deaths and 54,000 hospitalisations at USD 486 per DALY averted. Seasonal delivery could further improve dose efficiency. Analyses in Mozambique similarly demonstrated substantial potential health gains, although cost-effectiveness remained strongly dependent on intervention price and the cost-effectiveness threshold used. Overall, this thesis demonstrates that new RSV immunisation strategies could substantially reduce clinical and economic burden, but their value and feasibility are context-dependent. Integrating local epidemiology, healthcare utilisation, costs and implementation characteristics into economic evaluations can make estimates more relevant for national decision-making. Health economic evidence can thereby support priority setting and resource allocation, while successful and equitable implementation ultimately also depends on affordable pricing, sustainable financing and health-system readiness.

title: B-249 Leveraging Routine Laboratory Parameters for Pediatric Respiratory Infection Triage: A Two-Stage Interpretable Machine Learning Approach for Differentiating Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Influenza
abstract: Abstract Background Pediatric respiratory tract infections (RTIs), primarily caused by influenza and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), remain a global health priority. During peak seasons, the co-circulation of multiple pathogens makes clinical differentiation based on symptoms alone difficult. While routine laboratory tests—such as complete blood count (CBC) with integrated whole-blood C-reactive protein (fastCRP) analysis and basic biochemistry—are standard, their multidimensional diagnostic potential through machine learning (ML) has not been fully realized for rapid pathogen-specific triage. To develop and validate an interpretable two-stage ML framework that utilizes routine laboratory parameters to screen for broad respiratory infections and subsequently differentiate between influenza and MP in children. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 8,504 clinical records from 2020 to 2024. After applying rigorous exclusion criteria—including individuals aged 18 years or older, recent COVID-19 infection, underlying immunodeficiencies, asthma, allergic diseases, immunosuppressive therapy, and incomplete laboratory data (missing CBC or biochemistry)—a refined cohort of 2,499 pediatric patients was utilized. The diagnostic workflow was structured as a two-stage cascade architecture. Stage 1 focused on distinguishing "negative" individuals from infection-positive patients. Negative cases were defined as those testing negative for 13 common respiratory pathogens: Influenza A (H1N1 and H3N2), Influenza B, Adenovirus, Bocavirus, Rhinovirus, Parainfluenza, Coronavirus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Metapneumovirus, MP, Chlamydia, and SARS-CoV-2. Patients identified as positive with a single-pathogen infection (specifically MP or Influenza) proceeded to Stage 2, which aimed to differentiate between these two most prevalent types. To address the significant class imbalance between the influenza group (n=133), MP group(n=475) and the negative control group (n=1,891), random undersampling was implemented during training. The modeling process utilized Random Forest (RF) for Stage 1 and LightGBM (LGBM) for Stage 2, selected after comparing performance against XGBoost and Logistic Regression. Feature selection involved a rigorous consensus approach: candidate predictors were identified through LASSO regression, univariate logistic regression, and feature importance analysis, with final features determined via Venn diagram intersection. Model hyperparameters were optimized using cross-validation on the training set. Performance was evaluated using AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, with clinical interpretability provided by SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis. Results In Stage 1, six key features—including fastCRP Calcium, Phosphorus, Absolute Lymphocyte Count, Anion Gap (AG), and Basophil percentage—were identified, with the RF model achieving a recall of 0.7955. For Stage 2, four features—Monocyte percentage, Magnesium, RDW and AG—were selected. The final integrated cascade model demonstrated robust performance on the independent test set (AUC 0.8317; Accuracy 0.7551; Sensitivity 0.7083; F1-Score 0.7542). SHAP analysis revealed fastCRP as the primary predictor for Stage 1 screening, while Anion Gap (AG) emerged as the most discriminative feature for Stage 2 differentiation. Conclusion The proposed two-stage ML framework provides an interpretable and accessible tool for rapid pediatric triage. By integrating the significant predictive value of integrated whole-blood CRP for initial infection screening with routine metabolic markers like Anion Gap for MP and influenza differentiation, this study demonstrates a cost-effective, data-driven approach for enhancing clinical decision-making in laboratory medicine.

title: Immune transcriptomic differences in paediatric patients with SARS-CoV-2 compared to other lower respiratory tract infections
abstract: Abstract Background The clinical severity of SARS-CoV-2 infection in children varies, with asymptomatic or mild illness predominating and a minority developing severe disease. However, studies of the transcriptional responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection in children are limited. Understanding the immunological responses that underlie severity of disease may guide future development of preventive or therapeutic interventions. Methods Whole blood transcriptomes of healthy children ( N = 127) were compared to children with mild/asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection ( N = 71) and to children hospitalised with severe SARS-CoV-2 ( N = 41), lower respiratory tract illness (LRTI), LRTI due to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV-LRTI) ( N = 47), or Pulmonary Tuberculosis (PTB) ( N = 47). Results We identified > 5000 differentially expressed genes including: OLFM4 , IFI27 , CBX7 , IGF2BP3 , OTOF for severe SARS-CoV-2; IFI27 , OTOF , SIGLEC1 , IFI44L and USP18 for RSV-LRTI, and MMP8 , LTF , IGF2BP3 , GPR84 , CD177 , C1QC and DEFA4 for PTB, at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. Pathway analysis identified enrichment for neutrophil degranulation, interferon gamma signalling, overexpression of ribosomal proteins and depletion of immune response in severe SARS-CoV-2 compared to healthy (SAR-CoV-2 uninfected) children. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis ( WGCNA ) identified 10 correlated gene modules shared between LRTIs showing similar underlying response mechanisms. Cellular decomposition analysis identified the depletion of 22 cell types in severe SARS-CoV-2, 16 for RSV-LRTI and 21 for PTB compared to healthy children. Conclusion Severe COVID-19 in children exhibits a similar cellular response as previously reported in adults. We identified genes important for discriminating asymptomatic/mild from severe SARS-CoV-2, healthy children from severe SARS-CoV-2, RSV-LRTI and PTB, highlighting future therapeutic targets.

title: Predictors of intensive care unit admission in pediatric respiratory infections: the role of inflammatory indices and pathogenic profiles
abstract: Aim This study investigated clinical, laboratory, and respiratory pathogen-related factors associated with pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission among hospitalized children, emphasizing the role of inflammatory indices and the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII). Methods This retrospective study included children aged 1 month to 18 years hospitalized in the pediatric ward or PICU of Giresun University Women and Children Training and Research Hospital between January 2023 and March 2025. Eligible patients had at least one positive viral respiratory polymerase chain reaction (PCR) result. The primary outcome was PICU admission. We used multivariable binary logistic regression to evaluate associations between respiratory pathogens, clinical and laboratory parameters, and PICU admission. Results Among 835 patients, 291 (34.9%) required PICU admission. In the pathogen-based model, rhinovirus/enterovirus detection was independently associated with increased odds of PICU admission (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.604), whereas adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and influenza/parainfluenza were associated with lower odds. In the clinical/laboratory model (n = 655), higher SII values (aOR, 1.051 per 100,000-unit increase; 95% CI: 1.029–1.074), heart rate (aOR, 1.025 per beat/min increase; 95% CI: 1.015–1.035), and plateletcrit (aOR, 1.036 per 0.1% increase; 95% CI: 1.020–1.052) were independently associated with PICU admission, whereas higher albumin (aOR, 0.913; 95% CI: 0.876–0.951) and female sex (aOR, 0.667; 95% CI: 0.454–0.979) were inversely associated. SII discrimination was modest (area under the curve [AUC], 0.618). Conclusion Respiratory pathogen profile, SII, heart rate, plateletcrit, albumin, and sex were independently associated with PICU admission. These routinely available parameters may support early risk stratification when interpreted alongside clinical assessment.

title: Plasmonic biosensor platforms for next-generation personalized medical diagnostics
abstract: The increasing healthcare burden demands precise diagnostics for early detection and longitudinal disease monitoring. Although conventional assays such as ELISA and PCR offer precision, they require intensive sample preparation, bulkier instrumentation and prolonged assay times. This review examines plasmonic biosensors as a transformative alternative for personalized and point-of-care diagnostics. We comprehensively examine recent advancements, such as the integration of nanomaterials, microfabrication strategies, advanced surface chemistry and prototype miniaturization, and consider examples for the detection of cancer biomarkers (microRNA-21 and alpha-fetoprotein), viral proteins (respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2), and inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein). Furthermore, we address the critical aspects that hinder the clinical translation of plasmonic biosensors. The review concludes that, despite significant laboratory-scale progress, standardized manufacturing, scalable nanofabrication and the inclusion of artificial intelligence/machine learning frameworks remain essential for the widespread utilization of plasmonic technology in personalized medicine and diagnostics.

title_zh: 下一代个性化医疗诊断的等离激元生物传感器平台
source_body_en: The increasing healthcare burden demands precise diagnostics for early detection and longitudinal disease monitoring. Although conventional assays such as ELISA and PCR offer precision, they require intensive sample preparation, bulkier instrumentation and prolonged assay times. This review examines plasmonic biosensors as a transformative alternative for personalized and point-of-care diagnostics. We comprehensively examine recent advancements, such as the integration of nanomaterials, microfabrication strategies, advanced surface chemistry and prototype miniaturization, and consider examples for the detection of cancer biomarkers (microRNA-21 and alpha-fetoprotein), viral proteins (respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2), and inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein). Furthermore, we address the critical aspects that hinder the clinical translation of plasmonic biosensors. The review concludes that, despite significant laboratory-scale progress, standardized manufacturing, scalable nanofabrication and the inclusion of artificial intelligence/machine learning frameworks remain essential for the widespread utilization of plasmonic technology in personalized medicine and diagnostics.
abstract_zh: 日益增长的医疗负担要求精确的诊断以实现早期检测和疾病长期监测。尽管传统的检测方法如ELISA和PCR具有较高的精确度,但它们需要繁琐的样本制备、较大的仪器设备以及较长的检测时间。本综述探讨了等离激元生物传感器作为个性化和即时检测(point-of-care)诊断的变革性替代方案。我们全面审视了近期的进展,例如纳米材料的整合、微加工策略、先进的表面化学以及原型微型化,并考虑了用于检测癌症生物标志物(microRNA-21和甲胎蛋白)、病毒蛋白(呼吸道合胞病毒和SARS-CoV-2)以及炎症生物标志物(C-反应蛋白)的例子。此外,我们还讨论了阻碍等离激元生物传感器临床转化的关键因素。综述得出结论,尽管在实验室规模上取得了显著进展,但标准化制造、可扩展的纳米加工以及引入人工智能/机器学习框架仍然是等离激元技术在个性化医学和诊断中广泛应用所必需的。

title: An Autonomous Pathogen Detection System for Assessing Temporal Associations with Respiratory Pathogen Activity
abstract: Current respiratory pathogen surveillance is largely based on case reporting, sentinel surveillance, and environmental sampling. This study developed an autonomous pathogen detection system (APDS) integrating real-time bioaerosol sensing, intelligent triggering, aerosol collection, nucleic acid extraction, real-time PCR, and automated data reporting for respiratory pathogen surveillance. System performance was evaluated in a 20 m3 aerosol chamber and through 52 weeks of continuous monitoring in a hospital outpatient hall in Beijing. Laboratory experiments showed that the developed platform enables the detection of airborne influenza A virus at concentrations as low as 3.75 × 104 50% tissue culture infectious dose/m3 and can detect airborne Pseudomonas aeruginosa at concentrations as low as 1.80 × 104 copies/m3. The platform can detect low concentrations of airborne pathogen nucleic acids that are undetectable by surface sampling. During field monitoring, APDS autonomously triggered 381 tests and recorded 46 pathogen-positive detections. Respiratory syncytial virus showed significant correlations when APDS signals preceded national surveillance data by 1–3 weeks, with the strongest correlation at a 3-week lead (ρ = 0.487). Given the spatial mismatch between single-site APDS monitoring and national surveillance data, this association should be considered exploratory. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of APDS for long-term automated aerosol surveillance and suggest its potential as a complementary tool for respiratory pathogen monitoring.

title: Host-response biomarker panels for distinguishing selected acute respiratory viral-bacterial co-infections from mono-infections
abstract: Acute respiratory viral-bacterial co-infections complicate antimicrobial decisions because pathogen detection may not establish whether both organisms are clinically contributing to disease. We synthesized evidence from adult and pediatric acute respiratory infection cohorts, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and selected mixed-detection febrile illness studies, to evaluate host-response biomarkers for distinguishing co-infection from mono-infection. Conventional C-reactive protein and procalcitonin were most useful as supportive or rule-out markers of bacterial involvement, but lacked sufficient specificity when used alone. Dual-axis strategies that combine antiviral and bacterial-response signals, including MxA/CRP, TRAIL/IP-10/CRP, CD169/CD64, IFI44L/FAM89A, and targeted transcriptomic or proteomic signatures, provided more biologically coherent discrimination of mixed infection states. These findings support prospective validation of integrated host-response panels as rapid decision-support tools for antimicrobial stewardship and clinically meaningful co-infection diagnosis.

title: Duration and severity of asthma-like episodes in young children vary by viral and bacterial triggers.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Asthma-like episodes with cough, wheeze and/or breathlessness are frequent in young children and often triggered by respiratory tract infections. We aimed to examine whether specific microbial triggers of asthma-like episodes were associated with episode duration and severity. METHODS: We analyzed 453 nasopharyngeal aspirates collected during acute asthma-like episodes from 268 children aged 0-3 years from the COPSAC-2010 cohort. Samples were tested for common pathogenic respiratory viruses by PCR and for bacteria by culture. Asthma-like episodes were prospectively recorded in diaries. Associations between microbial triggers and episode duration and severity were analyzed by generalized estimating equations. Interactions between microbial triggers and selected asthma risk loci and polygenic risk scores (PRSs) were explored in relation to episode duration. RESULTS: Rhinovirus was associated with 27% longer episode duration compared to episodes without rhinovirus, predominantly driven by rhinovirus C (50% longer). Rhinovirus was also associated with a more than twofold increased risk of a severe asthma exacerbation (i.e., need for oral prednisolone, high-dose inhaled corticosteroids, and/or hospitalization) (OR 2.26; 95% CI 1.10-4.64; p = .027), with rhinovirus C exhibiting an even higher risk (OR 4.38; 95% CI 1.71-11.25; p = .002). Episodes with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and/or Moraxella catarrhalis were associated with 61% longer duration than episodes without these bacteria, which was particularly pronounced for M. catarrhalis (47% longer). In contrast, RSV; parainfluenza and influenza viruses were associated with shorter duration. Younger age correlated with longer episode duration and risk of a severe asthma exacerbation. Exploratory analyses suggested pathogen-specific interactions with selected asthma risk loci and asthma exacerbartion PRS in relation to episode duration. CONCLUSION: Specific microbial triggers and younger age were associated with the duration and severity of asthma-like episodes in young children. These findings may improve prognostic assessment and support more individualized management.

title: Generation and trial of mucosal virus vectored vaccines for bovine respiratory viruses
abstract: Bovine respiratory syncytial virus (bRSV) and bovine parainfluenza virus type 3 (bPIV3) are important components of the bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC), causing significant bovine morbidity and mortality. Current vaccine strategies arein efficient, and there is a clear need for novel vaccine candidates which subvert maternal antibody interference. Replication competent (rc) and replication incompetent (ri) Sendai virus (SeV) vectored vaccines expressing bRSV and bPIV3 surface glycoproteins were generated from their corresponding cDNA clone plasmids and characterised in vitro to confirm vector and heterologous protein expression. (rc) and (ri) vectored vaccines expressing bRSV heterologous proteins were taken forward for an immunogenicity study in mice, where bRSV specific IgG and mucosal IgA, as well as virus neutralisation capability, were investigated. Several promising vaccine candidates were identified which induced high levels of bRSV specific IgG and IgA, and significantly higher virus neutralisation antibody titres than controls. Thesis is embargoed until 31 July 2028.

full_text: AbstractIntroductionAlthough pneumococcal colonization is uncommon in adults, it may increase during respiratory viral infections. We investigated the frequency of pneumococcal colonization, associated factors, and serotype distribution in adults with confirmed respiratory viral infection.MethodsWe prospectively included adults presenting to the Emergency Department of Bellvitge University Hospital with influenza A virus (IAV), SARS-CoV-2, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, as well as 33 virus-negative controls (December 2023–January 2024). Nasopharyngeal swabs were tested for Streptococcus pneumoniae using a RT-PCR assay (lytA and piaB genes). Clinical data were analysed using Cox proportional hazards regression models.ResultsA total of 616 episodes were studied (IAV, n=391; SARS-CoV-2, n=162; RSV, n=28; >1 virus, n=35). Pneumococcal colonization was detected in 85 individuals, with the highest prevalence among IAV-infected patients (14.8%), followed by RSV (10.7%) and SARS-CoV-2 (9.3%). Individuals with viral infection showed higher pneumococcal loads (median lytA CT 23.1 [18.7–27.4]) compared to those without infection (CT 31.8 [31.5–33.3]). IAV (OR 3.52; 95%CI 1.30–9.17) and RSV (OR 4.04; 95%CI 1.11–13.50) were independently associated with pneumococcal colonization. Among adults <65 years, female sex (OR for male sex 0.43; 95% CI 0.19–0.90) was associated with colonization, whereas in those ≥65 years, RSV infection (OR 5.56; 95% CI 1.03–27.31) was the main association. Detected serotypes were diverse, predominantly non-PCV serotypes.ConclusionsPneumococcal colonization was more frequent during IAV or RSV than SARS-CoV-2 infection. In older adults, RSV infection showed a particularly strong association, highlighting potential implications for pneumococcal and RSV vaccination strategies.Keywords: colonization, IAV infection, pneumococcal vaccines, Streptococcus pneumoniae, viral infection 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study settingsThis study was performed at Bellvitge University Hospital, a referral hospital that attends adult patients (≥18 years old) at the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona (Spain). All patients with suspected respiratory viral infection are routinely screened through the Alinity m Resp-4-Plex assay (Abbott Molecular, US) and positive samples are frozen for further studies. In this work, we analysed all nasopharyngeal swabs that tested positive for IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and/or RSV from patients admitted to the emergency department between December 18th (2023) and January 18th (2024). For the analysis of pneumococcal load through real-time PCR, a selection of 33 samples that tested negative for viral infection during the same period were studied. Only one episode per patient was considered.2.2.Pneumococcal detection and serotypingNasopharyngeal samples were screened for the presence of S. pneumoniae as follows. DNA was extracted using the MagMAXTM Viral/Pathogen kit (KingFisherTM Flex purification system; Thermo Fisher Scientific). A multiplex real-time PCR (RT-PCR) was performed with the AgPath-ID one-step RT-PCR kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a QuantStudio 5 thermocycler (ThermoFisher, UK) using lytA and piaB genes as targets, with primers and probes previously described (Supplementary Table 1) (Carvalho et al., 2007; Trzciński et al., 2013). A sample was considered positive for S. pneumoniae when both targets tested positive with a cycle threshold value (CT) lower than 38 cycles and differed by no more than 3 CTs. Discordant results were resolved with a second RT-PCR targeting the SP2020 gene. Samples without amplification or only one positive target were considered negative (Tavares et al., 2019). Pneumococcal serotyping was performed with the S. PneumoStrip (Operon®) commercial kit, which detects 76 serotypes based on their genetic sequences. The method involves reverse hybridization, where amplified serotype-specific DNA sequences bind to probes on nylon membranes and are detected with a streptavidin-peroxidase conjugate (Ercibengoa et al., 2021).2.3.Clinical dataClinical characteristics were retrospectively collected, including age, sex, toxic habits, comorbidities (diabetes, chronic liver disease, chronic heart disease, COPD, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic renal failure, malignancies, immunosuppression and HIV infection), clinical presentation and 30-day mortality. Vaccination status regarding IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and S. pneumoniae was reviewed. For IAV, patients were considered vaccinated if received the seasonal 2023–2024 vaccine. Regarding pneumococcal vaccines, patients who received the PPSV23 polysaccharide vaccine within the last 5 years or a conjugate vaccine (PCV13 or PCV20) at any time but more than 14 days before the positive RT-PCR were considered vaccinated (Bonten et al., 2015). For SARS-CoV-2, all patients with at least one dose were considered vaccinated. Patients with no vaccination data in electronic records were considered unvaccinated.2.4.Statistical analysisTo study the factors associated with pneumococcal colonization, Cox proportional hazard regression models were estimated in the group of individuals with viral infection. The models were adjusted by age, gender, smoking, COPD, comorbidities, viral infection and vaccination status. The analyses were repeated stratifying by age groups (<65 and ≥65 years old). To study the factors associated with mortality, cox regression for each factor was estimated. These models were repeated adjusted by age, sex, viral infection (IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and RSV), pneumococcal colonization, comorbidities (chronic heart disease, malignancies and immunosuppression), clinical presentation (mild disease, hospitalization and respiratory failure) and vaccination status (SARS-CoV-2, IAV and S. pneumoniae vaccination). Because hospitalization violated the proportional hazards assumption (Grambsch and Therneau, 1994), we applied a time-varying methodology to adress this issue (Therneau and Grambsch, 2000). LytA CT values were compared between patients with and without viral coinfection using linear regression and visualized with violin plots. To assess the linear relation between lytA and piaB CT values, Spearman correlation and CI95% via bootstrap method was calculated. For data processing and analysis, R Studio (v4.4.1) and Python (v.3.12) were used.2.5.Ethics statementsThis work has been approved by The Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Bellvitge University Hospital (PR280/22) and it is in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki from the World Medical Association. Written informed consent was waived, as this was an observational study that used leftover isolates obtained during routine microbiological procedures. According to national normative data, all the data were anonymized, and patient confidentiality was always protected following the current legal normative in Spain (LOPD 3/2018 and RD 1720/2007). 3.1.Patients with Influenza A virus infection have higher rates of pneumococcal colonizationOver the study period, 616 episodes of respiratory viral infection were analysed. The most frequent virus detected was IAV (n=391, 63.5%), followed by SARS-CoV‐2 (n=162, 26.3%) and RSV (n=28, 4.5%). No Influenza B virus was detected. Viral coinfection was detected in 35 episodes, mostly IAV plus SARS-CoV‐2 (n=30, 4.9%). Detection of SARS-CoV‐2 plus RSV (n=4, 0.6%) and IAV plus RSV (n=1, 0.2%) was infrequent. There were no statistically significant differences between the CT values of the different viral infections, with median CT values of 25.0 (IQR 19.0-29.0), 25.5 (IQR 18.0-32.2) and 26.0 (IQR 22.0-31.0) for IAV, SARS-CoV‐2 and RSV, respectively. The median age of the studied population was 72.0 years old (IQR 55.0-81.0), and 300 episodes (48.7%) occurred in females. Compared to SARS-CoV‐2, infections caused by IAV or RSV occurred in younger people, and more frequently required hospital admission, although no statistical differences were found (Table 1; Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, SARS-CoV‐2 and RSV infections displayed higher rates of malignancies and immunosuppression. We investigated the frequency of pneumococcal colonization, associated factors, and serotype distribution in adults with confirmed respiratory viral infection.MethodsWe prospectively included adults presenting to the Emergency Department of Bellvitge University Hospital with influenza A virus (IAV), SARS-CoV-2, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, as well as 33 virus-negative controls (December 2023–January 2024). Nasopharyngeal swabs were tested for Streptococcus pneumoniae using a RT-PCR assay (lytA and piaB genes). Clinical data were analysed using Cox proportional hazards regression models.ResultsA total of 616 episodes were studied (IAV, n=391; SARS-CoV-2, n=162; RSV, n=28; >1 virus, n=35). Pneumococcal colonization was detected in 85 individuals, with the highest prevalence among IAV-infected patients (14.8%), followed by RSV (10.7%) and SARS-CoV-2 (9.3%). Individuals with viral infection showed higher pneumococcal loads (median lytA CT 23.1 [18.7–27.4]) compared to those without infection (CT 31.8 [31.5–33.3]). IAV (OR 3.52; 95%CI 1.30–9.17) and RSV (OR 4.04; 95%CI 1.11–13.50) were independently associated with pneumococcal colonization. Among adults <65 years, female sex (OR for male sex 0.43; 95% CI 0.19–0.90) was associated with colonization, whereas in those ≥65 years, RSV infection (OR 5.56; 95% CI 1.03–27.31) was the main association. Detected serotypes were diverse, predominantly non-PCV serotypes.ConclusionsPneumococcal colonization was more frequent during IAV or RSV than SARS-CoV-2 infection. In older adults, RSV infection showed a particularly strong association, highlighting potential implications for pneumococcal and RSV vaccination strategies.Keywords: colonization, IAV infection, pneumococcal vaccines, Streptococcus pneumoniae, viral infection
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study settingsThis study was performed at Bellvitge University Hospital, a referral hospital that attends adult patients (≥18 years old) at the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona (Spain). All patients with suspected respiratory viral infection are routinely screened through the Alinity m Resp-4-Plex assay (Abbott Molecular, US) and positive samples are frozen for further studies. In this work, we analysed all nasopharyngeal swabs that tested positive for IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and/or RSV from patients admitted to the emergency department between December 18th (2023) and January 18th (2024). For the analysis of pneumococcal load through real-time PCR, a selection of 33 samples that tested negative for viral infection during the same period were studied. Only one episode per patient was considered.2.2.Pneumococcal detection and serotypingNasopharyngeal samples were screened for the presence of S. pneumoniae as follows. DNA was extracted using the MagMAXTM Viral/Pathogen kit (KingFisherTM Flex purification system; Thermo Fisher Scientific). A multiplex real-time PCR (RT-PCR) was performed with the AgPath-ID one-step RT-PCR kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a QuantStudio 5 thermocycler (ThermoFisher, UK) using lytA and piaB genes as targets, with primers and probes previously described (Supplementary Table 1) (Carvalho et al., 2007; Trzciński et al., 2013). A sample was considered positive for S. pneumoniae when both targets tested positive with a cycle threshold value (CT) lower than 38 cycles and differed by no more than 3 CTs. Discordant results were resolved with a second RT-PCR targeting the SP2020 gene. Samples without amplification or only one positive target were considered negative (Tavares et al., 2019). Pneumococcal serotyping was performed with the S. PneumoStrip (Operon®) commercial kit, which detects 76 serotypes based on their genetic sequences. The method involves reverse hybridization, where amplified serotype-specific DNA sequences bind to probes on nylon membranes and are detected with a streptavidin-peroxidase conjugate (Ercibengoa et al., 2021).2.3.Clinical dataClinical characteristics were retrospectively collected, including age, sex, toxic habits, comorbidities (diabetes, chronic liver disease, chronic heart disease, COPD, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic renal failure, malignancies, immunosuppression and HIV infection), clinical presentation and 30-day mortality. Vaccination status regarding IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and S. pneumoniae was reviewed. For IAV, patients were considered vaccinated if received the seasonal 2023–2024 vaccine. Regarding pneumococcal vaccines, patients who received the PPSV23 polysaccharide vaccine within the last 5 years or a conjugate vaccine (PCV13 or PCV20) at any time but more than 14 days before the positive RT-PCR were considered vaccinated (Bonten et al., 2015). For SARS-CoV-2, all patients with at least one dose were considered vaccinated. Patients with no vaccination data in electronic records were considered unvaccinated.2.4.Statistical analysisTo study the factors associated with pneumococcal colonization, Cox proportional hazard regression models were estimated in the group of individuals with viral infection. The models were adjusted by age, gender, smoking, COPD, comorbidities, viral infection and vaccination status. The analyses were repeated stratifying by age groups (<65 and ≥65 years old). To study the factors associated with mortality, cox regression for each factor was estimated. These models were repeated adjusted by age, sex, viral infection (IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and RSV), pneumococcal colonization, comorbidities (chronic heart disease, malignancies and immunosuppression), clinical presentation (mild disease, hospitalization and respiratory failure) and vaccination status (SARS-CoV-2, IAV and S. pneumoniae vaccination). Because hospitalization violated the proportional hazards assumption (Grambsch and Therneau, 1994), we applied a time-varying methodology to adress this issue (Therneau and Grambsch, 2000). LytA CT values were compared between patients with and without viral coinfection using linear regression and visualized with violin plots. To assess the linear relation between lytA and piaB CT values, Spearman correlation and CI95% via bootstrap method was calculated. For data processing and analysis, R Studio (v4.4.1) and Python (v.3.12) were used.2.5.Ethics statementsThis work has been approved by The Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Bellvitge University Hospital (PR280/22) and it is in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki from the World Medical Association. Written informed consent was waived, as this was an observational study that used leftover isolates obtained during routine microbiological procedures. According to national normative data, all the data were anonymized, and patient confidentiality was always protected following the current legal normative in Spain (LOPD 3/2018 and RD 1720/2007). 3.1.Patients with Influenza A virus infection have higher rates of pneumococcal colonizationOver the study period, 616 episodes of respiratory viral infection were analysed. The most frequent virus detected was IAV (n=391, 63.5%), followed by SARS-CoV‐2 (n=162, 26.3%) and RSV (n=28, 4.5%). No Influenza B virus was detected. Viral coinfection was detected in 35 episodes, mostly IAV plus SARS-CoV‐2 (n=30, 4.9%). Detection of SARS-CoV‐2 plus RSV (n=4, 0.6%) and IAV plus RSV (n=1, 0.2%) was infrequent. There were no statistically significant differences between the CT values of the different viral infections, with median CT values of 25.0 (IQR 19.0-29.0), 25.5 (IQR 18.0-32.2) and 26.0 (IQR 22.0-31.0) for IAV, SARS-CoV‐2 and RSV, respectively. The median age of the studied population was 72.0 years old (IQR 55.0-81.0), and 300 episodes (48.7%) occurred in females. Compared to SARS-CoV‐2, infections caused by IAV or RSV occurred in younger people, and more frequently required hospital admission, although no statistical differences were found (Table 1; Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, SARS-CoV‐2 and RSV infections displayed higher rates of malignancies and immunosuppression. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionInflammatory conditions of the upper respiratory tract, such as viral infections, can promote the colonization of S. pneumoniae, which in turn may exacerbate the severity of the viral infection. This could partly explain the increased detection of S. pneumoniae during winter seasons, corresponding with higher circulation of respiratory viruses. The interaction between pneumococcus and viral infections has been classically described in the context of IAV infection, with evidence from murine models demonstrating increased pneumococcal load, supported by clinical data showing enhanced disease severity (Diavatopoulos et al., 2010; Mina et al., 2014; Wolter et al., 2014). Nevertheless, evidence of interactions between SARS-CoV-2 and S. pneumoniae remains limited. In fact, following the emergence of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, a global decrease in the incidence of pneumococcal diseases was observed, also in our area (Amin-Chowdhury et al., 2021; Calvo-Silveria et al., 2025). In this study, we explored the frequency of pneumococcal colonization and the factors influencing it in adult patients with respiratory infection caused by IAV, SARS-CoV-2, or RSV.Sample collection was conducted in Catalonia during the 2023–2024 winter season, coinciding with a high circulation of IAV. This was, in fact, the first winter season with substantial circulation of respiratory viruses other than SARS-CoV-2 since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. During the sample collection period, the estimated incidence of IAV infections ranged from 213 to 358 episodes per 100,000 population (https://sivic.salut.gencat.cat/, accessed July 2nd 2026), which was significantly higher than the estimated incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infections (70 to 156 episodes per 100,000 population). Therefore, it is coherent that IAV was the most prevalent virus detected. Regarding clinical data, differences based on the type of viral infection were observed, with patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 being older and exhibiting a higher prevalence of malignancies and immunosuppression. The observation that IAV infections affected younger individuals with fewer severe comorbidities might point to a greater severity of illness associated with IAV compared to SARS-CoV-2, as previously reported (Xue et al., 2022). However, it should be noted that the vaccination rate for SARS-CoV-2 was significantly higher than that for seasonal Influenza, which likely contributed to a greater proportion of mild infections. Indeed, more than 80% of vaccinated individuals (451/557) had received three or more doses of the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. This discrepancy not only highlights the success of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination programs in mitigating the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic but also underscores the urgent need to enhance seasonal Influenza vaccination uptake.Pneumococcal colonization is the critical step in the pathogenesis of pneumococcal diseases. While colonization rates are high among children under 5 years, they are substantially lower in adults (Palmu et al., 2012; Narciso et al., 2025). Despite lower colonization rates, older adults experience a high incidence of pneumococcal disease, which is partly attributable to age-related immunosuppression and the higher prevalence of chronic medical conditions (Grant et al., 2023). Nevertheless, our findings show not only an increased frequency of pneumococcal colonization among adults, which may reflect a population bias resulting from the overrepresentation of individuals with comorbidities, but also an elevated pneumococcal load in the context of viral infection. These findings could provide insight into the pathogenesis of pneumococcal pneumonia in adults, given that respiratory viral infections enhance pneumococcal overgrowth, predisposing the host to bacterial lung invasion and pneumonia development (Zhou et al., 2012). Moreover, this represents a potential source of pneumococcal transmission to other individuals in the community highlighting the role of adults in the maintenance and transmission of pneumococci. Interestingly, our study identified a high pneumococcal colonization rate among young adults, a population generally characterized by a low incidence of pneumococcal disease. In our cohort, a substantial proportion of young patients were immunosuppressed or presented with comorbid conditions. Additionally, smoking and alcohol abuse, recognized risk factors for pneumococcal disease among young adults (Grau et al., 2014), were notably prevalent within this population. These findings indicate that patients requiring healthcare due to acute respiratory viral infections, including older adults and young adults with comorbidities or risk habits, exhibit higher rates of pneumococcal colonization than the general population. Consequently, these groups represent important targets for respiratory disease prevention, particularly through vaccination.Regarding the viral-bacteria interactions, our data show a higher proportion of adults with pneumococcal colonization among infections caused by IAV or RSV. The pneumococcal load associated with IAV and RSV was also higher than that observed for SARS-CoV-2 infections. This suggests that interactions between pneumococci and respiratory viruses may be less significant in the case of SARS-CoV-2. Additionally, we observed notable age-related differences in the factors associated with pneumococcal colonization. Among young adults, female sex and infection with IAV virus were the factors most strongly associated with pneumococcal colonization. The higher propensity for pneumococcal colonization observed among females may reflect increased contact with children, a well-established risk factor for pneumococcal carriage (Wyllie et al., 2024; Almeida et al., 2025). In older adults, RSV infection was notably associated with an increased likelihood of pneumococcal colonization. Indeed, both IAV and RSV infections have previously been linked to the resurgence of pneumococcal diseases following the relaxation of non-pharmaceutical interventions due to the COVID-19 pandemic (Rybak et al., 2024). On the contrary, reported data seem to indicate that the rates of pneumococcal colonization remained stable (Danino et al., 2022; Wyllie et al., 2023). All these data suggest that the incidence of pneumococcal disease depends more on the triggering effect of IAV and RSV in promoting pneumococcal infection, rather than on a significant impact on colonization rates. The fact that pneumococcal and RSV interaction was observed mainly among older adults suggests that RSV may require additional host factors, such as more severe comorbidities, compared to IAV, to cause disease in the adult population (Ackerson et al., 2019). In any case, infections caused by IAV, RSV, or SARS-CoV-2 were associated with higher pneumococcal loads compared to cases without these viruses, suggesting that all three may contribute to promoting pneumococcal colonization (Brito-Mutunayagam et al., 2025). These findings underscore the importance of coordinated vaccination campaigns targeting both respiratory virus and S. pneumoniae to help mitigate the burden of epidemic peaks of respiratory infections in adults.Over the past years, multiple pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) have been introduced, mainly focused on paediatric immunization. Since 2023, several Autonomous Communities in Spain, including Catalonia, have recommended the use of the PCV20 for adults aged 65 years and older, as well as for individuals at increased risk. Our data show a low uptake of PCVs (<20%) among individuals aged 65 years and older, likely because the sample was collected during the first year of the program’s implementation. Regarding PCVs and viral infections, published evidence suggests that PCVs may have a beneficial role in preventing respiratory tract infections of viral origin, particularly those caused by IAV and SARS-CoV-2 (Lewnard et al., 2022; Lewnard et al., 2023).
