full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionStreptococcus pneumoniae infections are among the most frequent vaccine-preventable diseases worldwide (Toor et al., 2021). Pneumococcus colonizes the upper respiratory tract of humans, where it can persist and spread to other hosts. Colonization rates are high in children under 5 years old, reaching up to 50%, and are reported to be low in healthy adults (Weiser et al., 2018). Nevertheless, colonization rates in adults can be modified depending on some conditions such as chronic respiratory diseases, close contact with young children and the presence of respiratory viral infections (Almeida et al., 2021).Interactions between pneumococci and viral pathogens can facilitate the colonization and the transmission of S. pneumoniae, making seasonal respiratory viral infections key drivers in the spread of pneumococcus (Manna et al., 2022). Viral infections, as well as other inflammatory conditions of the respiratory tract, facilitate pneumococcal colonization and increase bacterial load, resulting in synergistic interactions that can exacerbate disease severity (Zhou et al., 2012). Indeed, co-infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae and respiratory viruses is associated with complications of the lower respiratory tract and poorer clinical outcomes (Liu et al., 2021). Among these, the interaction between pneumococci and Influenza virus (IAV) is one of the most thoroughly documented examples of bacteria-virus interplay, with a well-established impact on disease progression (Wolter et al., 2014). IAV has been shown to promote S. pneumoniae colonization in murine models (Mina et al., 2014), primarily through alterations in lung physiology, such as epithelial damage and surfactant dysfunction, that may create a favourable environment for subsequent pneumococcus superinfection, contributing to increased respiratory complications (McCullers, 2014). Similarly, in a human challenge study, pneumococcal colonization was associated with impaired mucosal immune responses to IAV vaccination, potentially facilitating the development of more severe disease (Carniel et al., 2021).Non-pharmacological COVID-19 containment measures, implemented to control the spread of SARS-CoV‐2, also led to a decrease in infections caused by other respiratory pathogens, including S. pneumoniae (Amin-Chowdhury et al., 2021). However, this reduction appears to reflect the decrease in seasonal viral infections rather than an actual reduction in pneumococcal carriage (Danino et al., 2022). In fact, the number of cases of pneumococcal invasive disease began to rise in several countries after relaxation of SARS-CoV‐2 control measures (Shaw et al., 2023; Rybak et al., 2024), returning to pre-pandemic levels in some regions (Hyams et al., 2023). In this context, the complex interplay between viral infections and pneumococcal diseases underscores the importance of ongoing surveillance and adaptive public health responses. For this reason, we aimed to explore the prevalence of pneumococcal colonization in adult patients presented to the emergency department with a respiratory viral infection due to IAV, SARS-CoV‐2 or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Specifically, our objectives were to analyse differences in the rate of pneumococcal colonization between viruses, describe the population of pneumococcal serotypes, and explore the clinical impact of pneumococcal colonization and vaccination status on viral respiratory infections. 2.1.Study settingsThis study was performed at Bellvitge University Hospital, a referral hospital that attends adult patients (≥18 years old) at the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona (Spain). All patients with suspected respiratory viral infection are routinely screened through the Alinity m Resp-4-Plex assay (Abbott Molecular, US) and positive samples are frozen for further studies. In this work, we analysed all nasopharyngeal swabs that tested positive for IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and/or RSV from patients admitted to the emergency department between December 18th (2023) and January 18th (2024). For the analysis of pneumococcal load through real-time PCR, a selection of 33 samples that tested negative for viral infection during the same period were studied. Only one episode per patient was considered. 2.2.Pneumococcal detection and serotypingNasopharyngeal samples were screened for the presence of S. pneumoniae as follows. DNA was extracted using the MagMAXTM Viral/Pathogen kit (KingFisherTM Flex purification system; Thermo Fisher Scientific). A multiplex real-time PCR (RT-PCR) was performed with the AgPath-ID one-step RT-PCR kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a QuantStudio 5 thermocycler (ThermoFisher, UK) using lytA and piaB genes as targets, with primers and probes previously described (Supplementary Table 1) (Carvalho et al., 2007; Trzciński et al., 2013). A sample was considered positive for S. pneumoniae when both targets tested positive with a cycle threshold value (CT) lower than 38 cycles and differed by no more than 3 CTs. Discordant results were resolved with a second RT-PCR targeting the SP2020 gene. Samples without amplification or only one positive target were considered negative (Tavares et al., 2019). Pneumococcal serotyping was performed with the S. PneumoStrip (Operon®) commercial kit, which detects 76 serotypes based on their genetic sequences. The method involves reverse hybridization, where amplified serotype-specific DNA sequences bind to probes on nylon membranes and are detected with a streptavidin-peroxidase conjugate (Ercibengoa et al., 2021). 2.3.Clinical dataClinical characteristics were retrospectively collected, including age, sex, toxic habits, comorbidities (diabetes, chronic liver disease, chronic heart disease, COPD, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic renal failure, malignancies, immunosuppression and HIV infection), clinical presentation and 30-day mortality. Vaccination status regarding IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and S. pneumoniae was reviewed. For IAV, patients were considered vaccinated if received the seasonal 2023–2024 vaccine. Regarding pneumococcal vaccines, patients who received the PPSV23 polysaccharide vaccine within the last 5 years or a conjugate vaccine (PCV13 or PCV20) at any time but more than 14 days before the positive RT-PCR were considered vaccinated (Bonten et al., 2015). For SARS-CoV-2, all patients with at least one dose were considered vaccinated. Patients with no vaccination data in electronic records were considered unvaccinated. 2.4.Statistical analysisTo study the factors associated with pneumococcal colonization, Cox proportional hazard regression models were estimated in the group of individuals with viral infection. The models were adjusted by age, gender, smoking, COPD, comorbidities, viral infection and vaccination status. The analyses were repeated stratifying by age groups (<65 and ≥65 years old). To study the factors associated with mortality, cox regression for each factor was estimated. These models were repeated adjusted by age, sex, viral infection (IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and RSV), pneumococcal colonization, comorbidities (chronic heart disease, malignancies and immunosuppression), clinical presentation (mild disease, hospitalization and respiratory failure) and vaccination status (SARS-CoV-2, IAV and S. pneumoniae vaccination). Because hospitalization violated the proportional hazards assumption (Grambsch and Therneau, 1994), we applied a time-varying methodology to adress this issue (Therneau and Grambsch, 2000). LytA CT values were compared between patients with and without viral coinfection using linear regression and visualized with violin plots. To assess the linear relation between lytA and piaB CT values, Spearman correlation and CI95% via bootstrap method was calculated. For data processing and analysis, R Studio (v4.4.1) and Python (v.3.12) were used. 2.5.Ethics statementsThis work has been approved by The Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Bellvitge University Hospital (PR280/22) and it is in accordance wit…
